AFG.story:
In August 2014 the Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission, a national body that monitors rights, finished a national inquiry into bacha bazi, the practice in which powerful men keep boys to dance for them and sexually abuse them. It held 71 focus groups and 17 public hearings in 17 provinces, attended by almost 2,200 people. Two-thirds of the victims said the men had paid them money. Its chair, Sima Samar, said Afghan law did not properly prevent the practice.

Some of the men keeping boys were commanders in Afghan forces that the United States supported. In 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases. Nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR), the official who audits US spending there, to investigate. SIGAR's report, made public in January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault. The Leahy Law requires the US to stop aiding units that commit such violations, but the Pentagon used an exception in it and in December 2015 approved continued funding for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.

Under the Taliban, now the de facto authorities, the UN verified sexual violence against 13 children in 2022, 12 in 2023 and 6 in 2024, and attributed most of it to the Taliban. In March 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs, religious schools, told the broadcaster RFE/RL's Radio Azadi that teachers pressed them into sexual acts. One said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, a senior Quran teacher, who only told the teacher to stop.

A UN report counted 6,836 Taliban-run madrasahs for boys in February 2024, and the authorities who run them are the ones the UN holds responsible for most verified cases. Childlight's 2026 update found no representative survey data for South Asia, so the number of children affected is not known.

BDI.story:
Burundi sends soldiers to peace operations run by the African Union and the United Nations. In 2014 Human Rights Watch, a research and advocacy group, reported on the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) after 50 interviews in Mogadishu, 21 of them with survivors. It documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by AU soldiers, mainly Ugandan troops at the mission's headquarters and Burundian troops at their own base. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases for medicine or aid. Interpreters arranged the soldiers' access to them, and some were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine.

In the Central African Republic, Burundian soldiers served with MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission there. UN data list allegations against Burundian personnel involving 46 children between 2014 and 2016. Two allegations about soldiers from Burundi and Gabon in the town of Dékoa led UN investigators to interview some 136 alleged victims, 48 percent of all victims the UN recorded in 2016. A peacekeeper can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them, and the UN itself can only send them home. The Secretary-General's 2017 report said the investigations by Burundi and Gabon were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges.

Inside Burundi, little reaches the international counts. In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which receives reports of online abuse material from technology companies, recorded 1,028 reports for Burundi.

The soldiers identified at Dékoa went home without charges, and the last UN report in this record described Burundi's own investigation as pending. Because only Burundi can try its soldiers, any case for the children they are accused of abusing depends on Burundi's government.

CAF.story:
Between December 2013 and June 2014, boys aged about 8 to 13 living in a camp for displaced people at M'Poko airport in Bangui, the capital, said soldiers had sexually abused them, often in exchange for food or money. Most of the soldiers they described belonged to Sangaris, a French army operation; others were Chadian and Equatorial Guinean troops. The UN recorded the boys' accounts in an internal report but did not pass it to the French authorities. A UN official, Anders Kompass, passed it on himself; he was suspended, and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity. The Paris prosecutor opened an inquiry in July 2014 that came to cover accusations by fifteen children. In January 2018 French judges dismissed the case for lack of sufficient evidence, citing inconsistencies in testimony, and no soldier was charged.

In December 2015 a review panel appointed by the UN Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps called the UN's handling a "gross institutional failure". It found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.

Allegations then came against MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in the country. Two allegations about soldiers from Gabon and Burundi in the town of Dékoa led to interviews with some 136 alleged victims, 48 percent of all victims the UN recorded in 2016, and press accounts said 41 troops were sent home without charges. In 2021 the UN withdrew all of Gabon's roughly 450 soldiers after further allegations. Peacekeepers can be tried only by the country that sent them.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country, 58 by the CPC armed coalition and 35 by government and pro-government forces, and the abduction of 141 children. That year MINUSCA also recorded 13 child victims of its own personnel.

The cases on record against foreign soldiers ended in a dismissal in France or with troops sent home. Children are now abused by armed groups, by forces on the government's side and by peacekeepers, and Childlight's 2026 update found no representative survey data for West and Central Africa to measure how many.

CIV.story:
In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department described how girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and from other West African countries are brought to Abidjan, the largest city, by distant relatives who promise them school or training. Once there, the girls are made to work as servants in homes, where they are open to sexual exploitation. The report said Ivorian women and girls are trafficked for sex especially in Abidjan.

The same report described traffickers from Nigeria who recruit women and girls with offers of jobs in shops and then exploit them in the country's gold-mining and cocoa regions. The report on Nigeria said organised groups, some linked to Nigerian cult organisations, move women and girls to mining regions in several West African countries, Côte d'Ivoire among them.

Little else is counted. Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa had too few representative surveys on online exploitation of children to be measured.

The trafficking of girls into homes and mining areas is described in yearly US reports, and no national survey in this record measures how many children it affects.

DNK.story:
In May 2011 the Godhavn Report examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other Danish state children's homes between 1945 and 1976. It found neglect and physical and sexual abuse, and that the psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld had given psychiatric drugs to about 22 percent of the boys at Godhavn. No prosecutions followed. In 2019 Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims. In 2020 the government ordered a second investigation, into særforsorgen, the state's special-care institutions for people with intellectual and physical disabilities. Published in March 2022, it found widespread abuse, including sexual assault, of children and adults placed there between 1933 and 1980, and that the state had not carried out systematic oversight. About 15,000 people with disabilities had been committed. The social affairs minister, Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil, apologised for the state in September 2023.

Denmark also took in children from abroad. Between 1970 and 1989, 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark from South Korea. In January 2024 the Appeals Board, the agency that supervises intercountry adoption, found "systematic illegal behaviour" on the Korean side, where weak rules let agencies alter children's identities in official papers, and large sums passed between agencies in the two countries. It found that two Danish agencies, DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp, knew the children's information was being changed. The same year DIA, Denmark's only remaining intercountry adoption agency, said it was shutting down.

In 1992 US Customs, in its first major case against abuse material on the internet, found Bamse, a Danish bulletin board with rooms for abuse images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own; working with Danish police, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. In 2025 Danish police led an operation against a platform run by a Danish man who sold AI-generated abuse material, and Europol, the EU police agency, noted the lack of national laws covering such material.

Denmark has apologised for abuse in its state institutions, no prosecutions followed the Godhavn Report, and adoptee groups say the 2024 report on Korean adoptions did not examine the Danish state's own role.

FRA.story:
Between 1971 and 1991, Fr Bernard Preynat, a priest in Lyon, was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts. Many of the cases had passed the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, so he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991, and in March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison.

In November 2018 the French bishops set up the Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church (CIASE). It surveyed the general population as well as church archives. Its report in October 2021 estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, and about 330,000 if lay people working for the church were included. It called the causes systemic.

In 2004 the FBI traced a surgeon in western France, Joël Le Scouarnec, downloading abuse images. In 2005 he received a four-month suspended sentence, and prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities. A warning to the health ministry in 2007 brought no action, and a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction. At his second trial he admitted abusing 299 victims between 1989 and 2014, mostly patients, many under anaesthesia, more than 250 of them under 15. In May 2025 he was sentenced to the maximum of 20 years.

In 2021 the government created CIIVISE, a commission on incest and sexual violence against children. In November 2023 it estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence in France each year. Under the law, rape of a minor can be prosecuted until 30 years after the victim turns 18; CIIVISE asked for the deadline to be removed, which had not been adopted when it reported. In April 2025 a parliamentary inquiry estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the state child welfare services, the ASE, are exploited in prostitution.

France now has national estimates of abuse in the church and in families, and its parliament has found children in state care exploited in prostitution. The deadline for prosecuting rape of a minor still applies.

HTI.story:
Between 2004 and 2007, soldiers of the Sri Lankan army contingent in MINUSTAH, the UN peacekeeping mission in Haiti, sexually exploited children in a ring that an Associated Press investigation later found involved at least 134 peacekeepers and at least nine children. In 2007 the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services, the UN's internal investigators, found that the abuse was frequent and took place at virtually every location where the contingent was deployed. Of the 950 Sri Lankan soldiers, 114 were accused and 108 were sent home. Only the country that sends a peacekeeper can prosecute them. Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts "consensual" and nobody was jailed; in 2016 one victim received a one-off ex gratia payment, a payment made without admitting liability.

Haiti also sent 13,986 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and many children lived in orphanages paid for from abroad. In 2017 the charity Lumos found that at least US$70 million a year went to about a third of Haiti's orphanages, from donors 92 percent of whom were in the United States, and that only 15 percent of orphanages were registered. It found that these donations drove the opening of orphanages, some run purely for profit, which recruited children from their families. In 2007 a centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting adoption to their families, after misleading the parents with payments. In 2019 the government's social welfare agency, IBESR, assessed more than 750 orphanages and identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in them.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 566 children, 411 of them by the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, compared with 41 girls in 2023. The 2025 US trafficking report said many trafficked children are restavek, children sent to work unpaid as servants in other families' homes, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased their risk of sexual exploitation.

None of the peacekeepers who abused children was jailed. Children in Haiti now face sexual violence by gangs, unpaid servitude in other homes and an orphanage system kept going by foreign donations.

IRQ.story:
On 3 August 2014 fighters of the group calling itself Islamic State (ISIS) attacked Sinjar, the home of the Yazidi religious minority in northern Iraq. They moved the people they captured in buses and trucks to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, including Badoush prison and the Galaxy wedding hall in Mosul, and then sent women and girls on to Raqqa in Syria. ISIS sold women and girls, some as young as nine, at markets and held them as sexual slaves, and it forced boys into its training camps. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria, a panel of UN investigators, found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

Armed groups still take children in Iraq. The UN verified the abduction of 18 children in 2022, 10 of them by ISIS and 4 by the Kurdish armed group HPG/PKK, and of 8 children in 2024, mostly to recruit and use them in armed groups.

Women and girls whose relatives are accused of ties to ISIS live in camps for displaced people. The 2025 US trafficking report said security and military officials allegedly exploit such families, including children, in exchange for documents. An international organisation reported in 2024 that officials coerced relatives of detained children into sex acts in return for security clearances or civil papers, and the government reported no action against them. The report said Yazidi survivors remain at risk of being trafficked again.

Thousands of the Yazidis taken in 2014 are still missing. Children in the camps depend for their papers on officials accused of demanding sex for them, and Childlight's 2026 update found no representative survey data for the Middle East and North Africa that would show how common this abuse is.

KHM.story:
In 1992 and 1993 the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), a UN mission of about 22,000 personnel, was based in the country. Its arrival was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls. The UN kept no thorough record of allegations at the time.

Svay Pak, a fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became a place where foreign men bought sex with children, most of them ethnic Vietnamese girls, many sold by poor families. Reports in 2002 described the trade there as driven by Western sex tourists who had come after Thailand cracked down on child prostitution. On 22 January 2003 police raided the brothels after advertising the raid in advance. Almost all the children had been moved, and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had been extorting money from the brothel owners. The government closed the Svay Pak brothels in 2005, and the trade moved to massage parlours and karaoke bars. In 2017 ABC News reported that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35 percent to 1 to 2 percent.

Cambodian children were also sent abroad for adoption. The American facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families from 1997 to 2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions, and the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. The US suspended adoptions from Cambodia in late 2001. In 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering, admitting she had falsified documents; she denied trafficking.

The 2025 US trafficking report said Cambodian and foreign men still sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, and that children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts.

The sale of children moved out of open brothels into less visible places. The same 2025 report said complicity by officials, including at senior levels, still prevents effective law enforcement.

MAR.story:
In December 2010 Moroccan police arrested Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, and in September 2011 a court sentenced him to 30 years in prison for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. On 30 July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned him as one of 48 Spanish prisoners, a gesture towards Spain. Galván left Morocco on an expired passport, with the authorities' knowledge, before the pardon was cancelled. People protested outside parliament in Rabat, and police dispersed them violently. On 4 August 2013 the king revoked the pardon, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Spanish police arrested Galván on 7 August 2013, and he was imprisoned in Spain to finish his sentence. A 2010 US diplomatic cable had reported an earlier case, in which the king in 2006 pardoned a Frenchman, Hervé Le Gloannec, convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh; he was released.

The 2025 US trafficking report said foreign nationals, mainly from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in Morocco's major cities, and that NGOs report tourists abusing children in Tangier in holiday rentals owned and managed by Europeans. It also reported alleged exploitation of children after the Al Haouz earthquake of September 2023. Moroccan courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024.

Moroccan soldiers serving with the UN missions in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo were named in UN tables of sexual exploitation and abuse allegations for 2015 and 2016. Under UN rules only Morocco can prosecute them.

Foreign visitors still abuse children in Moroccan cities, and the 2013 pardon was revoked only after public protest. Childlight's 2026 update found no representative survey data for the Middle East and North Africa, so how many children are affected has not been measured.

NPL.story:
In March 2007 the British newspaper The Daily Telegraph described baby-buying, bribes and the deception of birth families in adoptions from Nepal. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions. In November 2009, at the ministry's request, the Hague Conference on Private International Law, an intergovernmental body that writes treaties on family law including adoption, sent a mission to Nepal. Its report of February 2010 cited evidence that papers were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin and age, and that this continued under new rules adopted in 2008. It said the US$5,000 payment for each child and the US$10,000 annual agency fee gave strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care. Nepal sent 1,991 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022.

Inside Nepal, children's homes recruit children from poor families. In 2021/22 the National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered homes holding 10,905 children, and UNICEF estimates that about 85 percent have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by the homes, and researchers say the homes use the children to attract donations. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by a 2018 law.

Girls are also taken across the open border to India. Nepal's National Human Rights Commission estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and said poor screening at the border makes this hard to control. Traffickers recruit with offers of jobs or marriage and through online romance scams, and the 2025 US trafficking report raised serious concerns of official complicity. In 2015 police in Kolkata freed six young women trafficked from Nepal who all carried fake adult identity papers, which International Justice Mission, a charity that works with police, said traffickers issue to underage girls.

Adoption abroad was halted, and children are still moved into homes and across the border for money. Childlight found in 2026 that South Asia has no representative survey data on online exploitation of children.

PRY.story:
In October 2003 a law created Paraguay's Truth and Justice Commission (Comisión de Verdad y Justicia) to examine the dictatorship of 1954 to 1989, known as the Stroessner regime. After collecting more than 2,000 testimonies, it presented its final report on 28 August 2008. It concluded that the regime's repressive apparatus, its security forces, fostered sexual violence against women and girls, and that this reached its extreme in the "sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime". Young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts for the officers' use. The commission recorded that 10.8 percent of victims were minors at the time and noted that sexual violence was heavily under-reported. Amnesty International reported that girls as young as seven were believed to have been taken from their homes for senior military officers.

Paraguay has also been a place where clergy accused abroad could keep working. In 2002 the Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in the Diocese of Scranton, in the United States, of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved with his group to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general, the bishop's second-in-command, in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres that year, reportedly in part over the case, and Urrutigoity was moved to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted. The Paraguayan newspaper La Nación reported that at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

The 2025 US trafficking report described criadazgo, the practice of making children work as unpaid domestic servants in other families' homes, as a common form of trafficking in Paraguay. It estimated that 47,000 children are in criadazgo, most of them girls, and said many are highly vulnerable to sex trafficking.

The sexual slavery of girls by the dictatorship's officers is now part of Paraguay's official record. Today the largest group of children at risk that the sources count are the 47,000 living as servants in other people's homes.

SWE.story:
In February 2011 a Swedish government inquiry, Vanvårdsutredningen, reported on abuse and neglect in municipal children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980. It recommended a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who had suffered serious abuse, and the apology was made at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up in January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53 percent of them, with no right of appeal.

Over the same decades Sweden took in children from abroad for adoption. It received 9,051 children from South Korea between 1957 and 2005. In January 1975, when South Korea tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia, the Swedish ambassador urged it to keep sending children. Children also came from Chile, where they were taken from mainly poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died; from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, when "baby farms" bought or abducted babies from hospitals; and from Guatemala, where a 2009 government study found that the army and police had moved children into the adoption system during the armed conflict. After activism by Chilean adoptees, Sweden opened its own inquiry. Its report of 2 June 2025, nearly 1,600 pages long, reviewed 65 years of adoption and documented numerous irregularities and illegal acts of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea.

Abuse material is also hosted on Swedish servers. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, took action against 6,820 internet addresses in Sweden, 2 percent of its total. In 2016 Europol, the EU police agency, said that at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 1,000 of them in Sweden, and that some had been sexually exploited.

Sweden's 2025 inquiry confirmed that state authorities had some knowledge of irregular and illegal adoptions over decades. No source used here records what became of the 1,000 unaccompanied children who disappeared in Sweden.

TUR.story:
In March 2016 police in Karaman, a city in Türkiye, arrested a teacher for abusing 10 children in student houses, two of which belonged to the Ensar Foundation. On 24 March 2016 the Grand National Assembly, Türkiye's parliament, voted unanimously to set up a research commission on child abuse. By July its only field visit had been to Karaman, where the provincial family directorate, the local office for family affairs, gave members a report that blamed the victims' families. Its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, that people working with children have background checks, and that the legal definition of sexual abuse be widened. Members from the opposition party CHP said the report was general and theoretical and that the commission had not visited state nurseries, prisons or Syrian camps.

According to the 2025 US trafficking report, Türkiye hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians. The report said Syrian girls in Türkiye are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then held in domestic servitude and trafficked for sex. It said corruption and official complicity remained significant concerns and that no investigations of complicit officials were reported. In 2007 the US State Department had reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation to countries including Turkey.

In December 2025 prosecutors in Ankara reportedly opened an inquiry after an opposition MP, Turhan Çömez, cited files released by the US Justice Department. Among them was a 2009 civil complaint alleging, "upon information and belief", that Jeffrey Epstein brought minor girls from Turkey and other countries. No findings or charges have been reported.

The parliamentary commission did not visit the Syrian camps, and the forced marriage of Syrian refugee girls continues with no reported investigation of the officials involved.

ZWE.story:
From 1946 to 1956 the British Fairbridge Society sent 276 child migrants to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College in Southern Rhodesia, as Zimbabwe was then called, under a British child migration scheme. In 2018 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), the inquiry for England and Wales, found that children who told the headmaster that a padre, a chaplain, at the college had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against "spreading malicious lies".

In 1984 John Smyth, a British barrister, moved to Zimbabwe. In England he had beaten and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps. A 1982 internal report, the Ruston Report, described the beatings, and the people who received it did not tell the police until 2013. In Zimbabwe Smyth founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. A 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992, and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged. In 2024 the Makin Review, an independent review, called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa" and found no evidence of any effort to alert the Zimbabwean authorities.

In August 2021 a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a shrine of the Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect. On 24 September 2021 the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation. It found compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging (promising a girl as a future wife) and forced marriage in the Marange sect. A 2020 probe near Marondera had found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as "wives-in-waiting" and married at puberty. By 2022 the commission had investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation.

The 2025 US trafficking report said children are trafficked for sex around gold and diamond mines, and that ngozi, the practice of giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing, makes girls vulnerable. It said low-level officials were complicit.

The Gender Commission called for a law to regulate faith-based organisations, and no such law is recorded in the sources used here. Girls remain at risk around the mines and under ngozi.
